summary.case_overview: The judgment delivered by R. F. Nariman, J. on March 24, 2015, in a batch of writ petitions filed under Article 32 of the Constitution of India (headed by Shreya Singhal v. Union of India), addresses the constitutional validity of Section 66A, Section 69A, and Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, along with their related rules, as well as Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act, 1960 [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 18] [Page 19] [Page 20] [Page 21] [Page 102]. The Supreme Court evaluated these provisions primarily against fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(2), Article 14, and Article 21 of the Constitution of India [Page 1] [Page 24] [Page 35] [Page 98]. The Court declared Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act unconstitutional, upheld Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, and saved Section 79 and Rule 3(4) of the 2011 Intermediary Guidelines Rules by reading them down [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 112].
summary.facts_of_case: A batch of writ petitions were brought under Article 32 of the Constitution of India challenging the constitutionality of Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which was added by an Amendment Act of 2009 with effect from October 27, 2009 [Page 18] [Page 20]. Section 66A created a criminal offence for sending grossly offensive, menacing, or false information causing annoyance, inconvenience, danger, obstruction, insult, injury, criminal intimidation, enmity, hatred, or ill will via a computer resource or communication device [Page 20]. The petitioners also brought challenges against Section 69A of the IT Act and the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009; Section 79 of the IT Act and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2011; and Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 21] [Page 102] [Page 106] [Page 107].
summary.legal_issues: Whether Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 violates the fundamental right to free speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and whether it is saved as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2) of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 20] [Page 35]. Whether Section 66A is void for vagueness and overbreadth, creating a chilling effect on free speech [Page 1] [Page 11] [Page 24] [Page 81]. Whether Section 66A violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating arbitrary discrimination against internet users compared to users of other communication media [Page 1] [Page 24] [Page 98]. Whether Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act falls within the legislative competence of the State Legislature and whether it is constitutionally valid under Article 19(1)(a) [Page 2] [Page 102] [Page 104] [Page 106]. Whether Section 69A of the IT Act and the 2009 Blocking Rules are constitutionally valid and contain sufficient procedural safeguards [Page 1] [Page 14] [Page 106] [Page 108]. Whether Section 79 of the IT Act and Rule 3(4) of the 2011 Intermediary Guidelines Rules are valid or require reading down [Page 2] [Page 15] [Page 107] [Page 110].
summary.important_arguments_or_content: Counsel for the petitioners argued that Section 66A casts an excessively wide net over all information disseminated over the internet, directly impacting the public's right to know and failing to distinguish between mere discussion/advocacy and incitement [Page 4] [Page 24]. They submitted that Section 66A has no proximate nexus to any of the eight permissible subjects listed under Article 19(2), lacks defined terms, suffers from vagueness and overbreadth, and causes a total chilling effect on free speech [Page 4] [Page 8] [Page 11] [Page 35]. They further contended that Section 66A lacks procedural safeguards available under Sections 95, 96, and 196 of the Cr.P.C. [Page 13] [Page 99] [Page 101] and infringes Article 14 by discriminating against internet speech [Page 24] [Page 98]. The Additional Solicitor General, defending the statutes, argued that there is a presumption of constitutionality and that the legislature is best placed to appreciate societal needs [Page 24]. He submitted that internet communication differs fundamentally from print or broadcast due to its speed, global reach, potential for anonymity, ease of privacy invasion, and rumor propagation [Page 5] [Page 41]. He further argued that the possibility of statutory abuse is no ground to strike down an otherwise valid law and assured that the Government would administer Section 66A reasonably [Page 12] [Page 24] [Page 93] [Page 95]. Regarding Section 69A and Section 79, petitioners contended that procedural rules lacked adequate pre-decisional hearings for originators and forced intermediaries to exercise subjective self-censorship over user content [Page 106] [Page 108] [Page 110]. Regarding Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act, it was submitted that the State Legislature lacked legislative competence under Entry 31 of List I [Page 102] [Page 104].
summary.court_reasoning: The Court reasoned that freedom of speech and expression involves three fundamental concepts: discussion, advocacy, and incitement [Page 3] [Page 29]. Mere discussion or advocacy of an unpopular cause is protected under Article 19(1)(a), and restrictions under Article 19(2) apply only when speech reaches the level of incitement [Page 3] [Page 29]. Section 66A fails because it takes within its sweep protected and innocent speech without any proximate connection to public order, defamation, incitement to an offence, or decency/morality under Article 19(2) [Page 6] [Page 7] [Page 8] [Page 35] [Page 44] [Page 45]. Expressions used in Section 66A (such as 'grossly offensive', 'menacing', 'annoyance', and 'inconvenience') are open-ended, undefined, and vague, leaving citizens without fair notice and creating a chilling effect that leads to overbreadth [Page 8] [Page 10] [Page 11] [Page 74] [Page 76] [Page 83] [Page 90]. An assurance from the Government of reasonable administration cannot save an unconstitutional law, nor is any part of Section 66A severable [Page 12] [Page 92] [Page 94] [Page 96]. However, the Article 14 challenge against separate internet offences failed because there is an intelligible differentia between speech on the internet and other communication media based on reach, cost, and platform features [Page 5] [Page 13] [Page 98] [Page 99]. Regarding the Kerala Police Act, the Court found the Act as a whole falls in pith and substance under List II Entry 2 (and List III Entry 1), but Section 118(d) is unconstitutional under Article 19(1)(a) for the same vagueness and overbreadth as Section 66A [Page 2] [Page 14] [Page 104] [Page 105] [Page 106]. Regarding Section 69A and the 2009 Rules, the Court held they are narrowly drawn with specific Article 19(2) safeguards, written reasons, review committees, and hearing requirements [Page 14] [Page 15] [Page 106] [Page 107] [Page 108]. Regarding Section 79 and Rule 3(4) of the 2011 Rules, the Court held that to avoid intermediaries exercising self-judgment, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(4) must be read down so that 'actual knowledge' requires a court order or notification by the appropriate government or its agency strictly conforming to Article 19(2) [Page 15] [Page 16] [Page 111] [Page 112].
summary.decision_or_conclusion: The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 in its entirety as unconstitutional for violating Article 19(1)(a) and not being saved under Article 19(2) [Page 1] [Page 8] [Page 112]. The Court declared Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act unconstitutional for violating Article 19(1)(a) [Page 2] [Page 14] [Page 106] [Page 112]. The Court held Section 69A of the IT Act and the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 to be constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 14] [Page 15] [Page 112]. The Court upheld Section 79 of the IT Act subject to reading down Section 79(3)(b) to mean that an intermediary must receive actual knowledge from a court order or notification by the appropriate government/agency relating to Article 19(2) grounds; Rule 3(4) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2011 was similarly read down and upheld [Page 2] [Page 15] [Page 16] [Page 112]. All writ petitions were disposed of accordingly [Page 3] [Page 112].

summary.simplified_explanation: The Supreme Court of India evaluated whether government restrictions on internet speech were constitutional. The Court held that Section 66A of the Information Technology Act violated the right to free speech because its vague words—such as 'annoying', 'grossly offensive', or 'inconvenient'—could easily cover innocent discussions and opinions, creating a chilling effect where people fear speaking freely online [Page 1] [Page 8] [Page 10] [Page 11] [Page 112]. The Court clarified that sharing or advocating unpopular views online is protected, and speech can only be restricted if it directly incites violence or public disorder [Page 3] [Page 29]. For similar reasons of vagueness, the Court struck down Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act [Page 14] [Page 106] [Page 112]. However, the Court upheld the Government's power to block specific online content under Section 69A because that provision contains strict procedures and written safeguards tied directly to national safety and public order [Page 14] [Page 15] [Page 106] [Page 112]. Finally, the Court protected internet intermediaries (like social media platforms and search engines) under Section 79 by ruling that they are only required to remove content when they receive a formal court order or government notification, rather than having to act as private judges of online speech [Page 15] [Page 16] [Page 111] [Page 112].
